blocks.text: This is a cake. Look at the pink top. Look at the little candles. Before it went in the oven, the cake was runny. It was thin like soup. Then it got hot. blocks.prompt: How a Cake Puffs Up
blocks.text: A cake starts out as batter. Batter is wet and runny. You can pour it. When you mix batter, you beat air into it. The air makes tiny bubbles. The bubbles are so small you cannot see them. Then the batter goes into the hot oven. The bubbles get warm. Warm gas spreads out and takes up more room. So every tiny bubble grows bigger. The whole cake lifts up. The oven also cooks the eggs and the flour. They turn firm and hold the bubbles in place. Now the cake will stay puffy when it cools. A cake is mostly air, held in a soft net.

blocks.prompt: The Gas That Lifts the Cake
blocks.text: Air is not the only thing that lifts a cake. Most cakes get help from a white powder called baking soda. Baking soda has a job. When it gets wet and meets something sour, it makes a gas called carbon dioxide. Sour things in a kitchen are called acids. Lemon juice is an acid. So is yogurt, and so is buttermilk. Mix baking soda with an acid and you get fizz. That fizz is gas. Here is the surprising part. The gas cannot make new bubbles. It can only slip into bubbles that are already there, the ones you beat in when you stirred. So the gas does not build the cake. It blows up bubbles that the mixing bowl already made. Baking powder is baking soda with a dry acid already mixed in. Add water and heat, and it fizzes on its own. Then the oven sets the cake. Egg and flour turn firm around the bubbles and hold them still. The cake keeps its shape even after it cools.

notes: A foam is gas trapped inside something soft

blocks.prompt: A Cake Is a Foam
blocks.text: Think about what a cake actually is. It is not solid. Break a piece open and you will see thousands of holes, each one a pocket of gas trapped in something soft. Scientists have a word for a material like that. It is a foam. Bread is a foam. A sponge is a foam. So is a cake, which is why one kind is even called a sponge. Making a cake is really the job of building a foam and then locking it in place. It happens in three steps. First you make bubbles. Beating butter and sugar together does this, because the sharp edges of the sugar crystals tear tiny pockets of air into the fat. Whipping eggs does it too. This step matters more than it sounds, because every bubble the finished cake will ever have is born here. Second you inflate them. Baking soda meets an acid and releases carbon dioxide. Water in the batter turns to steam. Both gases push into the bubbles that already exist and swell them, the way breath swells a balloon that is already there. Third you set the foam. As the oven heats the batter past about 160 degrees Fahrenheit, egg proteins tangle together and starch grains in the flour soak up water and stiffen. The soft walls between the bubbles harden into a net. The cake stops rising and holds. Get any step wrong and the foam fails. Too little mixing, few bubbles, flat cake. Too much gas, the walls tear and the middle sinks. A cake is a small piece of engineering that happens to taste good.

blocks.prompt: Why Everyone Has a Cake on Their Birthday
blocks.text: For most of history, a cake was not a birthday thing. It was barely even a cake. The word comes from the Old Norse kaka, and it arrived in English around 800 years ago meaning something small, round, and flat. Early cakes were closer to sweetened bread. The Romans baked a heavy layered thing of dough, cheese, and honey. Egyptian bakers sweetened their loaves with honey, because they had no other sweetener worth the trouble. None of it looked like the pink and frosted object you picture now. Three ordinary inventions changed that, and none of them were about cake. The first was cheap sugar. For centuries sugar was a luxury priced like a spice, kept in a locked box, shaved off a hard cone with special nippers. Through the 1800s it became cheap and ordinary, and a recipe that swallowed cups of it stopped being absurd. The second was baking powder. Before it, a baker who wanted lift had two options: whip eggs by hand until your arm gave out, or use yeast and wait. In 1843 an English chemist named Alfred Bird mixed baking soda with a dry acid and sealed them in a tin, because his wife could not eat yeast. Suddenly the gas came from a spoon. The third was the oven. A cake needs steady, moderate heat for a long time. Wood-fired brick ovens ran hot and then cooled, and bakers judged the heat by holding a hand inside. Ovens you could actually set to a number showed up in the early 1900s. After that, a cake stopped being a gamble. The candles came from somewhere else. The custom of one candle for each year of a child's life is usually traced to Germany in the 1700s, long before most families could bake the cake underneath them. The two habits met later, once the ingredients caught up with the ceremony. So the birthday cake is not an ancient tradition that survived. It is a new one, made possible by a cheap sweetener, a tin of powder, and a dial on an oven door.

6.title: The Cake That Is Mostly Air
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Cake That Is Mostly Air

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A cake is a solid foam
Bubbles are made in the bowl, not the oven
Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate
Rising and setting are a race
Sugar delays egg proteins from setting
Chiffon cake, invented 1927, was a change of fat
Staling is starch recrystallizing, not just drying

blocks.prompt: The Engineering of Cake: How to Trap a Gas in a Solid
blocks.text: A cake is a solid foam, which is a strange thing to eat. Foam means a gas trapped inside something else, held there in countless separate pockets. Break a slice open and the evidence is right in front of you: a honeycomb of holes, each wall a thin film of cooked egg, starch, and fat. A baker is not really making a food. A baker is making a structure and hoping it holds. The structure is built in a fixed order, and the first step is the one people misunderstand. Bubbles cannot be created by heat, and they cannot be created by baking powder. They have to be there first. When butter and sugar are creamed together, the hard edges of the sugar crystals cut through the fat and drag pockets of air in behind them. When eggs are whipped, protein unwinds and wraps around air. Every bubble the finished cake will ever contain is made in that bowl, at room temperature, before any heat is involved. Everything that follows can only enlarge what already exists. The enlarging is chemistry. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and when it meets an acid in a wet batter it breaks apart and gives off carbon dioxide. Baking powder is the same soda with a powdered acid packed alongside it, dry and inert until liquid arrives. Meanwhile the water in the batter turns to steam, which expands enormously. Both gases migrate into the existing air pockets and swell them from within. The batter climbs. Then comes the race. Rising and setting are two clocks running at once, and a cake succeeds only if they finish together. As the batter passes roughly 160 degrees Fahrenheit, egg proteins coagulate and starch granules swallow water and swell, and the liquid walls between the bubbles turn firm. If the walls set too early, the gas has nowhere to go and the cake is dense and tight. If the gas arrives too fast or the walls stay soft too long, the bubbles merge, break the surface, vent, and the middle collapses into the crater every home baker has produced at least once. The lesson is that a cake recipe is not a list of flavors. It is a set of instructions for controlling a race between two processes, and the ingredients are chosen for their timing. Sugar is a good example. It sweetens, obviously, but it also gets in the way of gluten forming, which keeps the crumb tender, and it raises the temperature at which egg proteins set, which buys the gas extra seconds to expand. Take the sugar out of a cake and you do not get an unsweetened cake. You get a different object entirely. Once you see cake as engineering, the inventions make sense. In 1927 an insurance salesman in California named Harry Baker worked out that liquid vegetable oil, unlike butter, stays soft when cold, and produced a cake so light that Hollywood restaurants bought every one he could make. He kept the method secret for twenty years before selling it to General Mills, who named it chiffon. His whole secret was a change of fat. Even staling is structural. A cake left out does not simply dry. Its starch molecules, forced apart and softened by water in the oven, slowly creep back into orderly crystals, squeezing water out and turning the crumb firm. Warm the slice gently and some of those crystals loosen, and the cake goes soft again for a while. It was never about moisture leaving the room. It was about starch remembering its old shape.
